content.text: Our Solar System is our cosmic neighbourhood—a tiny corner of the Milky Way galaxy containing the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, and comets. Understanding the structure and scale of the Solar System helps us appreciate both Earth's place in the universe and the challenges of space exploration.
The Solar System contains the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, and comets. The Sun holds 99.8% of the total mass and its gravity keeps everything in orbit.
Contains 99.8% of the Solar System's mass
Asteroids (rocky objects, mostly between Mars and Jupiter)
Comets (icy objects from outer Solar System)

"The Sun is a big ball of fire"
— The Sun is a ball of plasma. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion, not burning.
— Vast distances separate planets. Even at light speed, journeys take minutes to hours.
— There's so much space that spacecraft pass through easily without hitting anything.
— Since 2006, Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet because it hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
"Earth is closest to the Sun in summer"
— Earth's seasons are caused by axial tilt, not distance. We're actually slightly closer in January (Northern Hemisphere winter).

Students often confuse asteroids and comets. Remember: asteroids are rocky objects mostly found in the asteroid belt, while comets are icy objects from the outer Solar System that develop tails when near the Sun.

Solar System: Sun + 8 planets + dwarf planets + moons + asteroids + comets
Sun: 99.8% of system's mass, powered by fusion
Inner planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (rocky)
Outer planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (gas giants)
Asteroids: rocky, mostly in asteroid belt
Comets: icy, develop tails near Sun
Solar System formed ~4.6 billion years ago from nebula
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
— ordered by increasing distance from the Sun (recall)
1 AU is the average distance from Earth to the Sun; 1 AU = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m
Inner planets are small, rocky, have few or no moons, and thin or no atmospheres. Outer planets are large gas/ice giants with many moons, ring systems, and thick atmospheres.
— e.g. Earth (rocky, 1 moon) vs Jupiter (gas giant, 79+ moons) (comparison)
— Time = 43 × 60 = 2580 s; Distance = 3 × 10⁸ × 2580 = 7.74 × 10¹¹ m; In AU: 7.74 × 10¹¹ / 1.5 × 10¹¹ = 5.16 AU (calculation)
Pluto has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit, which is one of three criteria required by the IAU definition of a planet (2006). It is now classified as a dwarf planet.
— orbits among other Kuiper Belt objects (reasoning)
The Sun is composed mainly of hydrogen (~73%) and helium (~25%). It produces energy by nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy.

Far from the Sun the comet appears as a small icy body with no visible tail. As it approaches the Sun, solar radiation and the solar wind cause surface ice to sublimate and dust to be released, forming a glowing coma and one or two tails (gas tail and dust tail) that point away from the Sun.
— tails always point away from Sun regardless of direction of travel (application)
